~12% of influenza cases that require hospitalization in the U.S. result in death (probably-ish).

It's just, most people don't catch it, and of those that do, only 5-10% need a hospital.

If you had a bunch of extra cases all in a bunch, more than you could test for and more than you could treat, you'd prefer to test (and then treat) the patients that showed up at the hospital in the worst condition...

If you had, say, hospitals at only half their max capacity & 5x the number of cases of "SARS-CoV-2-just-a-flugaloo" as of seasonal flu, you can admit 1x extra to the hospital but you've still got 4x the typical caseload of flu victims who will still need hospital care. So, the "gonna be okay, probably" hospital cases get triaged out in favor of the "this person WILL die w/out hospital care" cases.

Now, you've filled your medical system (with its limited testing & reporting capacity) with all the most dire cases. Suddenly, all the cases you measure are very deadly!

And, while that's all happening... other treatable conditions become formerly-treatable conditions (due to supply, hospital space, or doctor shortages) increasing total deaths (though not total deaths attributed to the virus if they're doing statistics properly).

It's the combination of high spread rate & high hospitalization chance, combined with the longer-than-normal hospital stay (up to 3 weeks) that make this so dangerous. Relative to the other pathogens going around.
